endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Organizations may choose to apply their existing risk tiering to GAI systems, or they may opt to revise or update AI system risk levels to address these unique GAI risks.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Health care practices and institutions should not utilize AI systems or technologies that introduce overall or disparate risk that is beyond their capabilities to mitigate.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Determine whether the use of the solution is consistent with the implementing organization’s risk tolerance and whether the solution offers an appropriate way to achieve stated goals in light of identified risks.

endorsements.title: The selective deployment of AI in healthcare: An ethical algorithm for algorithms
endorsements.quote: However, if the deployment of the DermAssist app would cause more overall harm than benefit to dark-skinned groups, there is a strong argument for selective deployment to light- skinned groups while more data is urgently gathered.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether declining or restricting AI tools after failed validation or excess risk reduces harm, and no study supplied documents the hazard of broad deployment of such tools. Five sources endorse the practice, four at a "should" level and one at a "may" level, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The five endorsements come from three frameworks, one guidance document, and one commentary, and none reports outcome data from a governance decision to decline or restrict a tool.

The endorsing sources differ in strength. The CHAI guides and the augmented intelligence principles use "should" language tied to organizational risk tolerance and mitigation capacity. NIST AI 600-1 uses "may" and leaves risk tiering to each organization. None of the supplied sources ties the practice to a specific statute or regulatory requirement.

The selective deployment commentary proposes restricting a dermatology app to light-skinned groups while more data are gathered. This approach limits exposure to a tool that may perform worse for dark-skinned patients, but it also withholds any benefit from them. No supplied study measures how restriction decisions affect access or outcomes across groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that follow governance decisions to decline, restrict, or conditionally deploy AI tools after failed or partial validation, and that compare patient harm, access, and performance gaps against broad deployment. Such studies should also describe what safeguards were attached to restricted use and whether staff adhered to the restrictions in practice.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The selective deployment commentary raises the possibility that restriction could shift benefits away from groups underrepresented in validation data, and health systems have no measured basis for judging how often that occurs.
